text:
0.1 How to read this book
Last updated: 2026-10-04 · Status: living document · Book version: tracks release 0.15.0
Sarathy is a personal AI assistant built to run locally, on the operator’s own hardware, against local models. This book is the engineering record behind it: how the system is put together, which patterns it leans on, and why each significant decision was made the way it was.
It is written for engineers, not for users. If you want to install and run the assistant, read the project README instead. If you want to know how the thing is built and why it is built that way, you are in the right place.
The chapters are meant to be read in order, but they are independent:

title: Sarathy Engineering
text:
0.2 House rules for this book
This book is destined for public hosting. Three rules are absolute, and they are enforced mechanically by the smoke test rather than by good intentions:

No personal information. No real names — the book says “the operator”, “the author”, “the user”. No chat identifiers, no contact details, no credentials of any kind.
No private paths. Everything is named relative to the repository root (sarathy/agent/loop.py) or relative to the workspace (workspace/sessions/). The machine’s home directories are never spelled out.
No private content. Nothing from the operator’s actual conversations, memory store or job records is quoted. The book describes mechanisms, never payloads.

Anything added to the book has to pass python3 -m unittest discover tests -k book, which scans both the .qmd sources and the rendered .html for the patterns above. See the update workflow in doc/README.md for how to add a chapter or a log entry.

0.3 Provenance: how claims in this book are sourced
Nothing here is invented. Every factual claim traces to one of four places, and the book says which:

The code. Repository-relative file paths and symbols, e.g. sarathy/session/manager.py (SessionManager._should_rotate).
The history. Commits are referenced by their short hash and subject, e.g. 67a3176 “rotate cron sessions at the trim cap”.
The operator’s engineering notes. A small number of decisions are not visible in the code at all — they are operational practice (how work is delegated, how releases are tracked). Those are drawn from the author’s notes and are labelled explicitly as such, because the repository cannot corroborate them.
Absence of evidence. Where the repository contradicts an expectation, the book says so rather than papering over it. For example, there is no in-tree text-to-speech pipeline; see the media-handling pattern in Chapter 3.

title: Sarathy Engineering
text:
0.5 Where to start
If you only read one diagram, read the system map in Chapter 2: one flowchart, one sequence diagram, and you understand the shape of the whole thing.
If you only read one chapter, read Chapter 4. Every design decision that cost something is written down there, including the ones that were wrong first.

title: 2  Why Sarathy Exists
text:
2.1 The problem, stated honestly
Personal AI assistants are, at the time of writing, mostly products rather than systems. They are large, opinionated, and — for the person actually trying to understand them — opaque. The author’s complaint, recorded in the project README, is specific and worth quoting as a design constraint rather than as a complaint:
That is the whole brief. Two words in it carry the engineering programme:
Those two words explain most of what follows in this book. A message bus with two dataclasses, rather than an event-sourcing framework, exists because the data flow must be legible. JSONL session files, rather than a document database, exist because a human must be able to read a conversation with cat. A Tool ABC with one execute() method, rather than a plugin marketplace, exists because “bloated” is the failure mode being engineered against.

title: 2  Why Sarathy Exists
text:
mainstream open implementations of this category are “heavily bloated and impossible for me to understand the data flow”; they “cater to all needs”.



“bloated” → build only the features actually used, and be able to delete the rest without ceremony. Every subsystem must justify its existence.
“data flow” → the operator must be able to trace any message end to end, by reading code, without a debugger or an observability stack. Traceability is a first-class requirement, not a nice-to-have.

title: 2  Why Sarathy Exists
text:
2.2 The starting point
Sarathy is a fork of nanobot, an existing minimal Python agent. Two other projects shaped the direction: nanoclaw, which demonstrated that a genuinely small assistant is enough for daily use, and a public argument for personalizing agents — assistants tuned to one person rather than to everybody.
Forking rather than starting from zero was a deliberate trade: inherit a working agent loop, message bus and provider layer, and spend the saved effort on the parts that are actually personal — memory, channels, sessions, scheduling. The cost of that trade is now visible in the tree: the fork’s shape (bus → loop → tools) is still the skeleton, and everything distinctive has been grown on top of it.
The name means helper, guide, driver, mentor in both Sanskrit and Tamil. It is chosen to describe the relationship the author wants with the tool: a driver who holds the map, not an oracle.

title: 2  Why Sarathy Exists
text:
2.3 From fork to independent architecture
The fork was a starting point, not a destination. Over 878 commits the package moved from “nanobot, lightly edited” to a system with subsystems that did not exist at all in the original:

Figure 2.1: Subsystems that exist today and did not exist in the starting fork. Each row is a commit range in the history, not a plan.





Four structural changes mark the transition from “fork” to “architecture”:

The gateway. The assistant stopped being a one-shot CLI and became a long-lived daemon (sarathy/gateway/run.py) that owns every subsystem in a single asyncio process. Lifecycle management (start/stop/restart/ status/logs) and log rotation came with it (sarathy/gateway/manager.py).
Channels as adapters. Telegram, Discord, Email, a web dashboard and — since 0.15.0 — a localhost-only backend trigger path all implement one interface (sarathy/channels/base.py) and speak two dataclasses. The agent stopped knowing which chat platform it was talking to.
Sessions became a subsystem. Append-only JSONL transcripts with a metadata header line, an LRU cache in front, a SQLite index beside them, and explicit archival with a verification stamp (sarathy/session/manager.py).
Learning became a pipeline. Memory writes used to race with each other from three different call sites; they are now produced by a single idle-time reviewer that refuses to run while the main model is busy (sarathy/session/review.py).

Each of those is documented in Chapter 2; the reasoning behind them is in Chapter 4.

title: 2  Why Sarathy Exists
text:
2.4 What “local-first” means here, concretely
“Local-first” is usually a slogan. In this repository it is a specific, checkable set of commitments:

Local models are the default, not a fallback. The default model in sarathy/config/schema.py is a local Ollama model; the provider registry (sarathy/providers/registry.py) carries exactly four kinds — Ollama, LMStudio, vLLM, and “any OpenAI-compatible endpoint” — and three of the four are local by construction.
No mandatory cloud service. There is no account, no signup, no hosted component in the happy path. Web search and speech-to-text have optional hosted providers behind configuration keys, and the assistant degrades cleanly when they are absent (sarathy/providers/transcription.py logs a warning and returns an empty transcript rather than failing).
One machine. The gateway, the database, the model server and the dashboard all live on the same host. The only inbound socket bound to anything other than loopback is the dashboard, and it is explicitly a LAN-reachable web UI with pairing-key authentication (sarathy/channels/dashboard/server.py).
Plain files as the substrate. Sessions, memory, skills, cron definitions and templates are all files you can open in an editor. SQLite appears only where a query surface genuinely earns it: the sessions index, the usage ledger, and the jobs ledger that the dashboard reads.
Stdlib-first Python. Requires Python 3.11+, ships as a single wheel, and leans on the standard library (asyncio, sqlite3, dataclasses, argparse-era pathlib) for the architecture; third-party libraries are used at the edges where they earn their place (LLM transport, chat-platform APIs, HTTP).

title: 2  Why Sarathy Exists
text:
2.5 What this project is not
Stated up front so the book is not read as a framework recommendation:

It is not a general-purpose framework. The README says so explicitly and declines feature requests and pull requests; the project exists as a working personal assistant that happens to be public.
It is not a research artifact. There are no benchmarks, no eval harness, no model comparisons. The success criterion is “the assistant works every day”.
It is not multi-tenant. Session keys are scoped to one operator’s channels. There is no concept of two users sharing a gateway.
It is not a place for secrets. Credentials live in the operator’s own config file, are never written to sessions, and are redacted before any config value is handed back over the dashboard API (redact_config in sarathy/channels/dashboard/auth.py).

title: 3  Architecture
text:
3.1 The system map
Sarathy is one asyncio process. Everything that can talk to the outside world — five channel adapters, the agent loop, the session store, the scheduler, the background reviewer, the heartbeat, and an embedded web server — runs inside a single event loop started by run_gateway() in sarathy/gateway/run.py.
That single decision is the source of most of the system’s simplicity: no IPC, no serialisation at the seams, no distributed tracing, and a data flow you can read end to end in one function.

title: 3  Architecture
text:
Adapters translate, they do not think. Every channel adapter turns its platform’s events into InboundMessage and its replies into OutboundMessage, and publishes them on one shared MessageBus. The agent never learns whether a turn came from a chat app, a browser tab, or a scheduled job.
The loop owns the turn. AgentLoop is the only component that calls the model, runs tools, or writes to a session.
State lives in files. Sessions, memory, skills and cron definitions are files in the workspace. SQLite appears in exactly three places, each of which needs a real query surface (see Chapter 3).

Then it does the only interesting thing structurally:

    agent.run(),        # consumes the inbound queue forever

agent.run() and the channel set are the two long-lived coroutines. Everything else — cron ticks, heartbeat ticks, background review, MCP connection setup — is a task spawned from one of them. Shutdown is symmetric: MCP exit stack closed, heartbeat stopped, cron stopped, agent stopped, channels stopped.

3.2.1 Process lifecycle
The daemon itself is managed by a thin wrapper, sarathy/gateway/manager.py: start spawns python -m sarathy.gateway.run --port N with start_new_session=True, writes the child’s PID to a file, and lets the child redirect its output to a timestamped log. stop sends SIGTERM. status probes the PID with signal 0 and clears the file if the process is gone. logs tails the newest log file, with --follow for tail -f behaviour.






stateDiagram-v2

  Absent --> Running: start
  Running --> Absent: stop / SIGTERM
  Running --> Starting: restart
  Starting --> Running: child healthy after 1s
  Starting --> Absent: child exited early
  Absent --> Running: restart (was absent)




Figure 3.2: Gateway lifecycle as exposed by the CLI. restart is a stop followed by a start; there is no in-place reload, because several subsystems hold process-wide state (see Chapter 4).





Note what is not here: no supervisor, no service manager, no container orchestration, no PID-file locking beyond the single file. The daemon is deliberately the simplest thing that survives a terminal closing.

title: 3  Architecture
text:
3.3 The message bus
Two dataclasses and two queues (sarathy/bus/events.py, sarathy/bus/queue.py):
@dataclass
class InboundMessage:
    channel: str
    sender_id: str
    chat_id: str
    content: str
    timestamp: datetime = field(default_factory=datetime.now)
    media: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    metadata: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)
    session_key_override: str | None = None

    @property
    def session_key(self) -> str:
        return self.session_key_override or f"{self.channel}:{self.chat_id}"
That session_key property is the load-bearing line of the whole design. Session isolation is not a policy enforced at the storage layer; it is a string computed once, at the edge, and carried by the message. Everything downstream — caching, archival, cost accounting, /stop targeting — keys off that string. If the channel layer computes the right key, the rest of the system cannot get it wrong.
metadata is the second load-bearing decision: it is the per-channel escape hatch. Message identifiers for threaded replies, image-provider role overrides, tool-hint flags, _progress markers, /btw markers, and usage-role overrides all travel as metadata rather than as new message types or new bus methods. The bus never learns a new concept.
OutboundMessage is smaller — channel, chat_id, content, reply_to, media, metadata — because the send path is genuinely uniform: look the channel up by name, call send().

Figure 3.3: One user message, end to end. Solid arrows are calls; the loop at the bottom is the only place the model is ever called.





Four things in that diagram are worth reading twice.
Permission is checked at the edge, once. BaseChannel._handle_message calls is_allowed(sender_id) and drops the message if the sender is not on the allow-list. The agent loop never re-checks, because it cannot be reached by anything that did not pass through an adapter.
Concurrency is layered, and the order is fixed. _dispatch() acquires, in order: the global lock (which guards runtime hot-reload, config mutations and the archival sweep), then a semaphore capping concurrent sessions (maxConcurrentSessions, default 4, clamped to 1..16), then the per-session lock. The rule “never hold a session lock while acquiring the global lock” is written into the code as a comment at the point where it would be violated.
The model is called from exactly one place. _run_agent_loop() is a while iteration < max_iterations loop around a single provider.chat() call. Everything that looks like an agent loop elsewhere in the system — cron runs, heartbeat ticks, /btw side turns, subagents — re-enters this same function. That is what makes the cost ledger, the usage footer, the steer injection point and the reviewer idle-gate work without special cases.
Progress is a message, not a channel. Long turns emit intermediate OutboundMessages carrying _progress (and optionally _tool_hint) metadata. The outbound dispatcher drops them unless the channel config asks for them (sendProgress, sendToolHints). Channels that support drafts rewrite the same message over and over; channels that do not simply ignore them.

title: 3  Architecture
text:
3.5 The agent loop, in detail
AgentLoop.run() is a poll loop with a one-second timeout so it can notice shutdown, plus three commands it intercepts before dispatching:

/stop — cancels every tracked task for that session key and every subagent spawned from it.
/steer — enqueues an instruction into the running session’s steer queue. The loop drains that queue at the top of every iteration, so a steer takes effect immediately after the current tool call returns, not after the whole turn. If the session is idle, the prefix is stripped and the text is dispatched as an ordinary message.
/btw — starts a genuinely concurrent second turn against a snapshot of the session, in its own ##btw## session, whose result is delivered when it is ready. It even saves and restores the message tool’s per-turn state so the side turn cannot pollute duplicate suppression for the main turn.

Everything else is dispatched as a task, tracked per session key, so that a slow turn in one chat never blocks another.
Inside _run_agent_loop(), per iteration, in this exact order:

Drain the steer queue and append any steers as synthetic user messages.
If a per-turn provider role was requested and images are present, hand the images to the provider tagged with the image role and rewrite the user message with a textual description (the “describe-then-inject” step).
Call the provider, streaming if the session or channel asks for it.
Record usage telemetry — always, and never fatally: a telemetry failure must not break a turn.
If there are tool calls: emit a tool hint, execute each one through the registry, append the results, and loop.
Otherwise stop, and let the caller apply topic markers, the usage footer and session persistence.

title: 3  Architecture
text:
3.6 Tools
A tool is a dataclass-shaped ABC with four members: name, description, parameters (a JSON schema) and async execute(**kwargs) -> str (sarathy/agent/tools/base.py). The registry turns that into OpenAI-style function definitions and enforces three things before the tool body runs (sarathy/agent/tools/registry.py):

schema validation of the incoming parameters, with a readable error listing which parameter was wrong;
a uniform error string, appended with an explicit instruction to the model to analyse the failure and try a different approach rather than repeating the same call;
registration order stability, so the cached prompt prefix does not churn.

The default set registered at construction time is: filesystem (read, write, edit, list), shell execution, web fetch, optional web search, message send, subagent spawn, cron (only when a scheduler is wired in), memory, and skill management. MCP servers, if configured, are connected lazily on the first turn and their tools are merged into the same registry, so the agent cannot tell where a tool came from.
Workspace restriction is enforced at tool construction, not at call time: restrict_to_workspace becomes the allowed_dir passed into the filesystem tools and the working directory for the shell tool.

title: 3  Architecture
text:
3.7 Sessions
SessionManager (sarathy/session/manager.py) is three cooperating things:

an LRU cache (OrderedDict, default 50 entries) of live Session objects, because a session is mutated in memory and flushed to disk opportunistically;
a JSONL file per session key, whose first line is a metadata record and whose remaining lines are messages — append-friendly, greppable, and readable by anything that speaks JSON;
a SQLite index (sessions/index.db) holding one row per session (key, channel, topic, timestamps, archived flag) so listing sessions is a single indexed query instead of reading every transcript.

A Session is deliberately a plain list of message dicts plus a metadata dict. get_history() slices the unconsolidated tail, aligns it to a user turn so the model never sees an orphaned tool result, and projects only the fields the API cares about. History is append-only for prompt-cache efficiency: nothing in the turn path edits or rewrites past messages.
Rotation happens in two places for two reasons. Session.add_message() rotates mid-turn when an interactive session reaches its size cap. get_or_create() rotates between turns for cron sessions, which must never rotate mid-run — see the 500-message hard lesson.
Archival writes a timestamped JSONL file into archived_sessions/, stamped archived: true only when the reviewer confirms it had no pending work for that session. Unstamped archives are re-verified once at gateway startup as crash recovery, and prune_archives() reaps old files while keeping anything still unverified, so a crash can never silently discard pending learning.

title: 3  Architecture
text:
3.8 Providers and hot reload
providers/registry.py holds a frozen table of provider metadata: name, keywords, environment variable, display name, LiteLLM prefix, whether it is local, and a default API base. Four kinds are supported — three local, one “anything OpenAI-compatible”. providers/manager.py turns a config entry into a client: direct HTTP client for OpenAI-compatible endpoints (which preserves reasoning content that LiteLLM would flatten), LiteLLM otherwise.
The interesting part is RuntimeProvider. It holds the live provider and model, and it re-reads the config file when — and only when — the file’s modification time changes:
def refresh(self) -> bool:
    mtime = self._file_mtime()
    if mtime == self._mtime:
        return False
    ...
Rebuilding the client only happens if the active provider, model, temperature, max tokens or reasoning effort actually changed. A failed rebuild keeps the old provider rather than dropping to no provider at all. Every turn calls runtime.apply_to(agent) under the global lock, which is why switching models from the dashboard or the CLI takes effect on the next message without a restart — while changing gateway source still requires a restart. The distinction is drawn on purpose; see Chapter 4.
Providers also carry roles (main, local, image), resolved per turn. A cron job payload can declare that it wants the local role, and the loop swaps the provider for that turn only, restores it in a finally block, and stamps the reply so the operator can see which provider ran it.

title: 3  Architecture
text:
3.9 The dashboard as a channel
The dashboard is not a separate service. DashboardChannel starts an aiohttp application inside the gateway’s own event loop (sarathy/channels/dashboard/server.py), serves the built single-page app, and exposes a REST API that operates directly on config, sessions and workspace files.

Two details are deliberate. First, the auth middleware validates pairing keys against the on-disk config on every request, so revoking a key from the CLI takes effect immediately instead of at the next restart; devices that pair successfully receive an opaque token whose hash is persisted, so a reconnect after a restart stays authenticated. Second, any config value whose key looks sensitive is replaced with a placeholder before the config document is handed back over the API, so the UI can render “set / not set” without ever receiving the value.

title: 3  Architecture
text:
3.10 The backend trigger path
Added in 0.15.0, sarathy/channels/backend.py is the one adapter that is not a chat platform. It exists so that programs — not people — can start a turn. It has two independent ways in:

a loopback-only HTTP endpoint that accepts a signed event envelope;
a tailer that polls a jobs database read-only for new rows in an events table and wakes a session per job.







flowchart LR
  subgraph producers["Event producers"]
    P1[Job runner]
    P2[Worker]
    P3[Operator tooling]
  end
  subgraph backend["BackendChannel"]
    E{{"POST /event<br/>token-gated"}}
    T["jobs.db tailer<br/>read-only, high-watermark"]
  end
  P1 --> E
  P2 --> E
  P3 --> E
  P1 -.->|"event rows"| T
  P2 -.->|"event rows"| T
  T --> F["filter by event type"]
  E --> N["InboundMessage<br/>session_key_override = backend:<job>"]
  F --> N
  N --> BUS[("MessageBus")]
  BUS --> LOG["log, or escalate_to channel"]
  style backend fill:#eef3f8,stroke:#3f6c99




Figure 3.5: The backend channel: two ways in, one isolated session out. Replies have nowhere to go, so they are logged, or escalated to a named channel when the envelope asks for it.





The security posture is conservative by construction, not by policy:

it refuses to start at all if no credential is configured;
a non-loopback bind address is forced back to loopback with a warning, so misconfiguration cannot expose it;
the token comparison is constant-time;
the jobs database is opened with SQLite’s read-only URI flag, so the tailer physically cannot write;
the tailer stores a high-watermark and, on first run, initialises it to the current maximum event id — history is never replayed into a session.

3.11 Where the state lives

    F1["workspace/memory/*.md<br/>capped, protected sections"]

  end
  subgraph sqlite["SQLite — only where queries earn it"]
    D1["sessions/index.db<br/>one row per session"]
    D2["usage.db<br/>append-only event ledger + epochs"]
    D3["jobs.db<br/>written by the job tooling, read by the dashboard"]

  SM["SessionManager"] --> F2 & F3 & D1

  style files fill:#eaf3ec,stroke:#5f8a6d
  style sqlite fill:#f7f0e6,stroke:#b08a3e




Figure 3.6: Storage by kind. Files are the default because they are inspectable; SQLite appears only where a query surface earns it.





The rule of thumb the codebase follows: if you would open it in a text editor to understand it, it is a file; if you would only ever query it, it is SQLite. Sessions and memory are files because reading a transcript is a real debugging need. The sessions index, the usage ledger and the jobs ledger are SQLite because nothing reads them by eye — they exist to answer questions, and a directory of JSONL files cannot answer “all sessions updated in the last week” without a scan.
Next: Chapter 3 takes the components above and names the patterns they implement.

title: 4  Patterns
text:
4.1 1. Channel adapter
A pattern is only worth naming if it comes with the rule that keeps it honest. Each section below gives the pattern, where it lives, and the invariant that prevents it from rotting.
Pattern. Adapter, over Strategy, over Plugin.
One abstract base class (sarathy/channels/base.py) with three abstract methods — start(), stop(), send() — and two concrete helpers every adapter inherits: is_allowed() and _handle_message(). _handle_message() is the important one: it is the only way an adapter is allowed to get a message onto the bus, so permission checking and dataclass construction happen in exactly one place.
classDiagram
  class BaseChannel {
    <<abstract>>
    +str name
    +start()
    +stop()
    +send(msg)
    +is_allowed(sender_id) bool
    #_handle_message(...)
  }
  class TelegramChannel
  class DiscordChannel
  class EmailChannel
  class DashboardChannel
  class BackendChannel
  BaseChannel <|-- TelegramChannel
  BaseChannel <|-- DiscordChannel
  BaseChannel <|-- EmailChannel
  BaseChannel <|-- DashboardChannel
  BaseChannel <|-- BackendChannel




Figure 4.1: The adapter seam. BaseChannel fixes the contract and the two invariants; the five concrete adapters only translate.
Invariant. A new channel never touches the agent loop, the session manager, or the bus internals. If adding a platform requires editing AgentLoop, the seam has leaked.
Two transport families, on purpose. Telegram and Discord are out-of-process clients (a polling thread and a websocket that must be reconnected). Email is pull-based (poll a mailbox on an interval). Dashboard and backend are in-loop aiohttp servers. Supporting all three shapes in one interface is the reason the interface is so small.

title: 4  Patterns
text:
4.2 2. Input-matched media
Pattern. Preserve the shape of the input in the output.
The agent is a text engine; the channels are not. The adapter’s job is to keep media typed end to end rather than flattening everything to text:

Inbound. An attachment is downloaded once, stored under the workspace media directory, and referenced by path on InboundMessage.media. Voice notes, audio, images and documents are distinguished by the platform payload, and images are additionally base64-inlined into the prompt as data URLs (ContextBuilder).
Outbound. OutboundMessage.media is a list of paths, and the channel maps each path to the right send call by extension — photo, voice, audio, or a generic document with the original filename preserved.

Two hard-won details are worth copying:

Name downloads by content, not by handle. Chat platforms hand out file identifiers that share a long common prefix across every attachment in a chat, so naming a download after a prefix of that identifier silently overwrote the previous attachment. The fix hashes the whole identifier and keeps the sender’s own filename as a readable prefix (commit e807552).
Do not fake what you do not have. There is no in-tree text-to-speech pipeline. Voice input is treated as media; a transcription provider module exists for callers that configure one, and it degrades to an empty transcript with a warning rather than failing the turn. The book says this explicitly rather than implying a voice round-trip that does not exist.

For images there is a third behaviour, “describe-then-inject”: when the active provider is tagged with the image role, the turn hands the images to that provider first and rewrites the user’s message with a textual description, so a small text-only main model can still reason about a screenshot.

title: 4  Patterns
text:
4.3 3. Session-key isolation
Pattern. Identity as a string, computed at the edge.
Every conversation is addressed by a channel:chat_id key. Three families exist and they are not interchangeable:








Key shape
Meaning
Rotation behaviour




telegram:<chat>, discord:<guild/channel>, email:<address>
A human conversation
Rotates when it reaches the size cap, mid-turn is fine


cron:<job>
One scheduled job, reused across every run
Never mid-turn; rotates between runs


backend:<job>
One job’s event stream
Isolated per job, never mixed with a chat


cli:direct, heartbeat, dashboard:console
Synthetic conversations
Ordinary interactive behaviour



Two escape hatches keep this from being rigid:

session_key_override on InboundMessage lets an adapter scope a session differently from channel:chat_id — thread-scoped chat sessions, and the backend channel’s per-job isolation both use it.
A generated side-conversation suffix (<key>##btw##<random>) gives /btw a real session of its own without inventing a new channel.

SessionManager derives the channel from the prefix (channel_for_key) and special-cases exactly one prefix for rotation (cron:). That is the entire policy surface.
Invariant. Two conversations never share a Session object. If a new integration needs shared context across conversations, it needs a different mechanism — not a shared key.

title: 4  Patterns
section: 4.4 4. Append-only transcripts with an index façade
text:
4.4 4. Append-only transcripts with an index façade
Pattern. Write-ahead log plus a derived index.
Sessions are JSONL files: line 1 is a metadata record, the rest are messages. That choice buys four things at once — append-only writes (so the prompt prefix stays byte-stable and provider prompt caches keep hitting), greppability, human readability, and trivial recovery, because a truncated file is still a valid prefix of a valid file.
The cost is that listing sessions means reading every file. That is what the SQLite index is for: one row per session, upserted on every save, rebuilt from scratch if it is missing. Reading the index is a fast path; reading the metadata lines is the fallback when the index is absent or empty.






flowchart LR
  CALL["list_sessions()"] --> TRY{"index present<br/>and non-empty?"}
  TRY -->|yes| Q[("SELECT ... FROM sessions<br/>ORDER BY updated_at DESC")]
  TRY -->|no| SCAN["read first line of<br/>each sessions/*.jsonl"]
  Q --> OUT["list of session records"]
  SCAN --> OUT
  UP["save() / archive"] -.->|"one cheap upsert"| Q
  style Q fill:#f7f0e6,stroke:#b08a3e




Figure 4.2: The façade. Callers ask for sessions; they never learn whether the answer came from the index or from a directory scan.





Two invariants keep the façade honest:

The index is never authoritative. If it disagrees with the files, the files win. rebuild_index() exists precisely for that case, and it runs automatically when the index file is missing at startup.
Writes are one row, best effort. A failed index upsert logs at debug level and never fails the save. The transcript is the data; the index is a cache.

Archival rotation. archive_session() writes a timestamped JSONL file and stamps it archived: true only when the reviewer confirms it has no pending work for that session. Unstamped archives are picked up by a one-shot sweep at gateway startup, and prune_archives() deletes old files while keeping anything still unverified. The result is that a crash between “archive” and “learn” cannot lose the learning.

title: 4  Patterns
text:
4.5 5. Skills as executable instructions
Pattern. Instructions as data, hot-reloaded, read on demand.
A skill is a directory containing a SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter and a Markdown body. It is not code and not a plugin; it is an instruction the agent chooses to read. Three sources are merged with a fixed precedence — global, then workspace, then built-in, with later sources overriding earlier ones.
The prompt never carries skill bodies. It carries a compact, generated summary: one line per category, the member names, and an availability flag derived from the skill’s declared requirements (a CLI on PATH, an environment variable present). The agent then reads the full SKILL.md with the file tool when it decides the skill applies.






flowchart LR
  subgraph sources["Skill directories"]
    S1[global skills]
    S2[workspace skills]
    S3[built-in skills]
  end
  MGR["SkillManager<br/>in-memory registry"] --> W
  W["watchdog observer<br/>(thread)"] --> Q["queue"]
  Q --> RELOAD["reload skill, run on_reload callbacks"]
  RELOAD --> CMD["CommandManager sync<br/>slash commands refresh"]
  RELOAD --> MGR
  MGR --> SUMMARY["compact skills summary<br/>injected into the prompt"]
  MGR --> READ["read_file(SKILL.md)<br/>when the agent decides"]
  S1 --> MGR
  S2 --> MGR
  S3 --> MGR
  style W fill:#f7f0e6,stroke:#b08a3e




Figure 4.3: Skill discovery and hot reload. The file watcher is the only long-lived thread-like thing in the system, and it hands work to the event loop through a queue rather than touching state itself.





Invariant. Editing a skill never requires restarting the gateway, and adding one never requires re-running an install step. The watcher debounces per file over a one-second window (editors write files twice), then hands the event to the event loop through a queue — the watcher thread never mutates the registry itself.
Why watchdog, not watchfiles. The project depends on watchdog and not on watchfiles; this is stated in the README as a deliberate choice. The practical reasons are that watchdog exposes the underlying filesystem events (so the code can filter to SKILL.md and debounce by path), it has no Rust-backed native wheel to build, and it composes with a plain queue hand-off into asyncio. The choice is about control over the event stream, not throughput.
Skill-first discipline. Skills are executable instructions, not documentation: read the file, then run the script it names, then record what happened. The built-in skills ship with real shell scripts (for example the tmux helpers) precisely so that “run the script” is a real instruction rather than an aspiration.

title: 4  Patterns
section: 4.6 6. Memory: capped files with protected sections
text:
4.6 6. Memory: capped files with protected sections
Pattern. Bounded buffer with a protected region.
Long-term memory is two small Markdown files — facts and user profile — with hard character budgets (2200 and 1375 characters by default). Small on purpose: these files are injected into every system prompt, so their cost is paid on every turn. When the budget is exceeded, trimming is not “drop the oldest line”:

the HARD LESSONS section is identified and preserved through any trim;
remaining sections are trimmed from the oldest inward, keeping the first section and the most recent ones;
only if that is still too large does the protected set get narrowed.

Two more invariants:

Check before writing. The memory tool refuses a write that would exceed the budget, and refuses an entry that is already present. Dedup is search-then- update, never append-and-hope.
One writer at a time. An asyncio.Lock guards writes to both files, and appends are atomic read-modify-write under that lock.

Idle-time review, not parallel review. BackgroundReviewer (sarathy/session/review.py) enqueues a snapshot after each turn and processes it only when the model is idle, with a cooldown and a busy counter rather than a boolean so that a side turn running alongside a main turn keeps the gate closed until every active model call finishes. The reason is stated in the module docstring: parallel model calls would degrade performance on local models, which is the whole point of running locally. Failed reviews are retried up to a bound and re-queued at the back so one bad snapshot cannot block the queue.

title: 4  Patterns
text:
4.7 7. Schedules as data
Pattern. Declarative payload, single store, explicit lifecycle.
The scheduler (sarathy/cron/service.py) keeps every job in one JSON file and computes the next run time from the last run time, not from “now”, so recurring schedules do not drift. It supports three schedule kinds — one-shot absolute, fixed interval, and a cron expression with an optional IANA timezone — and it validates the combination at add time so an invalid pair fails at the CLI rather than silently never firing.






flowchart LR
  T["timer armed for the<br/>earliest next_run"] --> DUE{"due?"}
  DUE -->|no| T
  DUE -->|yes| RUN["_execute_job(job)"]
  RUN --> CALL["on_job(job)"]
  CALL --> LOOP["agent.process_direct(<br/>session_key = cron:<job>)"]
  LOOP --> DELIVER{"deliver and target set?"}
  DELIVER -->|yes| OUT["publish_outbound"]
  DELIVER -->|no| DASH["dashboard notification"]
  RUN --> STATE["update last_status / last_error"]
  STATE --> NEXT["compute next run from last run"]
  NEXT --> SAVE["save job file"]
  SAVE --> T
  style LOOP fill:#eef3f8,stroke:#3f6c99




Figure 4.4: One scheduler tick. The job payload is the single source of truth for a run: message text, delivery target, and which provider role should execute it.





Two behaviours are worth stating because they are easy to get wrong:

Missed runs are caught up at startup, not silently skipped, but the next run for recurring schedules is then recomputed so a long outage does not produce a burst.
The in-memory store is the working copy. Mutations take an asyncio.Lock and re-save the file, but the file is only read once at load. This is the behaviour that produced the restart discipline in Chapter 4 — the scheduler is the one component where an external edit is a genuine foot-gun.

title: 4  Patterns
text:
4.8 8. Jobs as a queryable ledger
Pattern. Structured events, not log scraping.
The job tooling that runs alongside the assistant writes every task to a SQLite database: one row per job with a status enum and a spec/result path, plus a job_events table forming a timeline of structured events. Two consumers read it, both read-only:

the dashboard’s /api/jobs endpoints, which join the last event and an event count per job, and serve the spec and result text for the detail view;
the backend channel’s tailer, which wakes an isolated session when an event of an interesting type appears.

Completion is detected by the producer writing a done-marker file, not by a monitor grepping log output. That is a design choice with a large blast radius: log scraping is unparseable, races with log rotation, and produces false positives when a model quotes the phrase it was looking for. A file whose existence is the contract cannot be misread.
Invariant. Consumers open the database with SQLite’s read-only URI flag. The dashboard and the tailer physically cannot corrupt the ledger, which is what makes it safe to serve it over HTTP.

title: 4  Patterns
section: 4.9 9. Telemetry that cannot break a turn
text:
4.9 9. Telemetry that cannot break a turn
Pattern. Fire-and-forget instrumentation with schema migrations.
Every model call records a row into usage.db: tokens, cached tokens, completion tokens, cost, duration, finish reason, model, provider, channel, session key and epoch. The store is a lazy module-level singleton with thread-local connections, WAL journaling and a busy timeout, and it carries a real migration ladder (user_version 1 → 2 adds cost, 2 → 3 adds the session epoch) that is idempotent and re-checks the columns for fresh databases.
Two invariants:

Recording never raises into the turn. Usage capture is wrapped so that a telemetry failure is logged and the turn continues.
Tests never touch the production ledger. An autouse fixture points the store at a per-test temporary database and resets the singleton around every test, and the store itself has a second safety net that diverts to a temporary database whenever it detects it is running under a test.

This is a small pattern with a large payoff: it is why the assistant can afford to measure everything without adding a failure mode to the thing being measured.

title: 4  Patterns
text:
4.10 10. Verify before you close
Pattern. Definition of done includes the check.
This is the pattern that governs how work happens, not just how code is structured, and it has three parts:

Tests are part of the change, not a follow-up. Each behaviour in this book — session rotation, topic markers, backend envelopes, usage epochs, concurrency ordering — arrived with its test in the same commit.
The check is run by the person closing the work. Green is not claimed from a previous run; a suite that was flaky is re-run before it is believed, and if it is still flaky that is recorded as a defect rather than retried until it passes.
The artifact is inspected, not assumed. A handoff report is evidence, not proof; the finished thing is opened and walked.

The same discipline shows up inside the product: the dashboard’s session list has a fallback path precisely so that a missing cache degrades instead of lying, and the backend tailer refuses to replay history it cannot vouch for.

title: 4  Patterns
text:
4.11 11. Spec-first work
Pattern. One document per unit of work.
Coding work is delegated to headless coding agents, and the contract is a single Markdown spec per unit: goal, verified context, precise scope, explicit constraints, a definition of done, and a progress tracker that a resumed run reads before doing anything. The agent is told to ground every claim in the repository, and the report at the end must contain evidence, not adjectives.
Four rules make delegation safe rather than merely fast:

Free models only. Delegated runs use free-tier models. This is a hard rule, not a preference.
Verify before close. Whoever finishes the unit re-runs the tests, exercises live endpoints, and inspects the output before declaring it done.
One agent per repository, serialized. Two agents editing the same checkout is a lost update waiting to happen.
Restart the gateway after landing on gateway source. Configuration changes hot-reload; code changes do not. The rule that distinguishes the two is in Chapter 4.

title: 4  Patterns
text:
4.12 12. Restart discipline
Pattern. Make the correct action the easy action, and name the wrong one.
Changing source and changing configuration are different operations, and the system refuses to blur them:

Source change → a redeploy script: reinstall the package, write a restart-request flag, restart the daemon through the CLI, then confirm with a boot notification that carries version and provider status. The flag is consumed by the new process at startup, which is how the operator learns what is now live.
Configuration change → the CLI restart command, or nothing at all if the subsystem hot-reloads (the runtime provider does; the scheduler does not).

What is explicitly forbidden is killing the process by pattern from inside a session. A recorded incident cost roughly eight minutes of downtime because the kill pattern matched the shell command that was running it, severing the session that was doing the killing. The operational rule is now written down: restart through the CLI, never by hand.
Next: Chapter 4 tells the story behind each of these patterns — including the ones that were wrong first.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
text:
5.1 1. Local-first, and what that forbids
Every entry here has the same shape: the situation, the options that were real, the choice, and what the choice cost. Entries marked [ops] are operational practice from the operator’s engineering notes; the repository cannot corroborate them, and they are labelled so a reader can tell the difference.
Situation. Mainstream assistants in this category are cloud products with large dependency surfaces. The author wanted an assistant that runs on one machine and can be understood end to end.
Options considered. (a) Extend a general framework; (b) keep the dependency list small and support local model servers only; (c) local-first with hosted escape hatches where they are genuinely better.
Choice. (c), with a strong bias toward (b). The provider registry supports four kinds — three local, one “any OpenAI-compatible endpoint” — and nothing requires an account. Web search and speech-to-text may use hosted providers, but both degrade to a warning when unconfigured.
Cost. Features that assume a strong hosted model are simply absent. Reasoning effort is opt-in because not every local model supports it. The image provider role exists because a text-only main model cannot read a screenshot.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
text:
5.2 2. Fork, then diverge
Situation. Build a personal assistant. Write one from scratch, or start from something that already works?
Choice. Fork an existing minimal Python agent and keep its skeleton — bus, loop, tools — while growing a different architecture around it.
Why. The fork’s shape is genuinely good for this problem: a message bus, a tool loop, a provider layer. There was no reason to rewrite those. Everything the project is actually about — channels, sessions, memory, scheduling, a web UI, a job ledger — did not exist in the starting point and now constitutes most of the code.
Cost. Over 878 commits the divergence is total: the channel layer, session management, the gateway lifecycle, the dashboard and the backend trigger path are all new. The fork is now ancestry rather than architecture. What remains of the original is the shape of the turn loop and the module layout, both of which have been heavily extended.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
text:
5.3 3. One process, one event loop
Situation. The system needs a web dashboard, a chat bot, a scheduler, an IMAP poller and a model client. Each could be its own process.
Options considered. (a) Multi-process with IPC; (b) one process with threads; (c) one asyncio process hosting everything, including the HTTP servers.
Choice. (c).
Why it works. The dashboard’s aiohttp app and the backend channel’s app run inside the gateway’s event loop. There is no serialisation between the web request that starts a turn and the turn itself: the request handler publishes an InboundMessage and returns. A websocket frame and a cron tick travel the same path a Telegram update does. Threads are used in exactly one place — the skill file watcher — and it hands work back to the loop through a queue.
Cost. One slow blocking call in the loop stalls everything. This is why the heavy model listing and context-length detection run in a thread or behind short timeouts, and why the reviewer is gated on model idleness instead of running concurrently.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.4 4. Channels as adapters over a two-dataclass bus
text:
5.4 4. Channels as adapters over a two-dataclass bus
Situation. Five very different integrations need to reach the same agent.
Rejected first. Giving the agent a channel-specific entry point, or inventing a richer event hierarchy per channel.
Choice. Two dataclasses and two queues. InboundMessage and OutboundMessage, with a free-form metadata dict on both.
Why. The bus stays two concepts wide forever. Anything new a channel needs — thread identifiers, image roles, progress flags, side-conversation markers — travels in metadata instead of widening the bus. Session identity is a property computed on the message, so every downstream subsystem agrees on it for free.
Cost. metadata is untyped, and the consequences of that are handled by convention: keys are underscore-prefixed for internal markers, and every consumer that reads one documents what it expects. A wrong key fails quietly. This is a deliberate trade of static safety for extensibility in a system with exactly one integrator.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.5 5. A SQLite knowledge base instead of markdown-only memory
text:
5.5 5. A SQLite knowledge base instead of markdown-only memory
[ops] This decision lives in the operator’s workspace tooling, not in the package, so it is described as practice.
Situation. Markdown memory files are pleasant to read and edit by hand, but they stop working as a knowledge base past a few hundred facts: recall is substring matching, everything is in every prompt, and consolidation turns into guesswork about what to merge.
Choice. Durable facts live in a SQLite database with full-text search, behind a small command-line interface. The Markdown memory files are demoted to indexes — short, human-readable pointers into the database — rather than being the store.
Why. Search becomes a query instead of a grep, dedup becomes search-then-update instead of eyeballing, and the index files stay small enough to be injected into a prompt without cost. The single-writer discipline that follows from a CLI is the point: every durable fact enters through one path, so there is no question about who wrote what or when.
Cost. A fact that is not in the database does not exist, including for the operator. The CLI is a hard dependency of the workflow, and the index files drift if they are edited by hand — which is exactly why they are treated as generated.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.6 6. Idle-time review instead of a background thread per session
text:
5.6 6. Idle-time review instead of a background thread per session
Situation. The agent should learn durable facts from conversations. Commit 9046c87 records the earlier design: three writers — a per-message suggestion hook, a periodic consolidation pass, and a periodic archival pass — all writing the same memory file, producing duplicate entries and lost writes.
Choices. (a) Fix the races; (b) keep one writer but run it concurrently; (c) keep one writer and run it only when the model is idle.
Choice. (c), and the reviewer refuses to start while any model call is in flight.
Why. The concurrency is not the interesting constraint — the hardware is. Two simultaneous calls to a local model server halve throughput for the user’s own conversation. Idle-time review costs the user nothing and still runs after every turn.
Crash safety. The compromise this creates is that a session can be archived before its review finished. That is handled explicitly rather than ignored: the archive is stamped archived: false, a one-shot sweep at gateway startup re-processes anything still unstamped and then flips the stamp, and the archive pruner refuses to delete unstamped files. Learning is at-least-once, and the dedup check before each write makes that safe.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
text:
5.7 7. watchdog over watchfiles
Situation. Skills must hot-reload without a restart.
Choice. watchdog’s Observer with a custom event handler, not watchfiles.
Why. The handler receives raw filesystem events, which makes two things easy that would otherwise need extra machinery: filtering to SKILL.md only, and debouncing per path. The handler runs on a watchdog thread and does nothing but push (event_type, path) onto an asyncio.Queue; all mutation happens on the event loop, so the registry is never touched from two threads. It is also a pure Python package with no native wheel to build, which matters for a tool whose whole premise is “install it and it works”.
Cost. The debounce window is a hand-rolled one-second timer rather than a library feature, and the observer’s lifecycle has to be managed explicitly on start and stop.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.8 8. A compact skills summary instead of inlined skills
text:
5.8 8. A compact skills summary instead of inlined skills
Situation. Skills are Markdown documents. Inlining them all into the system prompt would be expensive and would blow the context on a small local model.
Choice. Generate a compact summary — category, count, availability, member names — and let the agent read the full SKILL.md with the file tool when it decides the skill applies.
Why. Skill discovery becomes cheap and constant-size, while skill content is paid for only when used. Availability is computed from each skill’s declared requirements so the summary tells the model what is actually runnable on this machine, not merely what is installed.
Cost. The agent has to make a decision to spend a tool call. A skill with a weak name or description simply never gets read; the summary line is therefore the most important text in the file, not the body.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.9 9. Session epochs: cost accounting that survives “start a new chat”
text:
5.9 9. Session epochs: cost accounting that survives “start a new chat”
Situation. Usage is recorded per session key. But a session key is reused across the whole life of a chat, so “how much has this conversation cost?” grows without bound and /new does not reset it.
Choice. Add an epoch counter, persisted per session key. Every usage row carries the epoch that was current when it was recorded, and a new conversation advances the epoch.
Why. Cost can then be reported per conversation rather than per key, with no destructive deletion of history — the ledger stays append-only and the usage_sessions table holds the authoritative current epoch, so a crash between “advance” and “next turn” cannot desynchronise. The footer shows the session cost at the current epoch.
Cost. One more dimension in every usage query and one more migration step (schema version 3). The epoch is resolved once per turn, not per record, so the hot path stays cheap.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.10 10. The 500-message cap and what a long-lived cron session did about it
text:
5.10 10. The 500-message cap and what a long-lived cron session did about it
Situation. Sessions are trimmed to a configurable cap — 500 messages by default — when saved to disk. Cron jobs reuse a stable per-job key, so their session is truncated forever and never grows past the rotation threshold.
The failure. Because the trim kept the file at the cap, the rotation check never fired. The session was reused indefinitely on a rolling window of stale context until a run’s prompt blew past the model’s context, at which point the run silently produced nothing and still reported success. Commit 67a3176 records the fix and the reasoning.






flowchart TB
  ADD["add_message()"] --> Q1{"interactive<br/>session?"}
  Q1 -->|yes| R1{"messages >=<br/>rotation cap?"}
  R1 -->|yes| ARC["archive + fresh session"]
  R1 -->|no| KEEP["append"]
  Q1 -->|no| KEEP
  GOC["get_or_create()<br/>between turns"] --> Q2{"cron session?"}
  Q2 -->|yes| R2{"messages ><br/>trim cap?"}
  R2 -->|yes| ARC
  R2 -->|no| KEEP
  Q2 -->|no| R3{"messages >=<br/>rotation cap?"}
  R3 -->|yes| ARC
  R3 -->|no| KEEP
  style ARC fill:#eaf3ec,stroke:#5f8a6d




Figure 5.1: Rotation policy after the fix. Interactive sessions may rotate mid-turn; cron sessions rotate only between runs, so a run in progress is never interrupted.





The rule that came out of it.

Cron sessions never rotate mid-turn — a rotation in the middle of a run would destroy the run’s context.
Cron sessions rotate between runs, at the trim cap, on both the cached path and the cold-load path (a session loaded from disk after a restart may already be over the threshold).
Cron sessions are exempt from the save-time trim, with a generous safety cap instead, so the archive captures their full history rather than a rolling window.
Archives get an explicit retention policy, because nothing else reaps them.

The generalisable lesson. A cap and a rotation threshold are different numbers. When a trim keeps a value below the threshold that triggers rotation, the rotation is dead code that nobody notices until the context explodes.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.11 11. The scheduler caches jobs in memory, so restart discipline became a rule
text:
5.11 11. The scheduler caches jobs in memory, so restart discipline became a rule
Situation. The scheduler reads its job file once at startup and keeps the job list in memory, re-saving the file on every mutation.
The failure. Editing the job file from outside — by hand, or with a script that was not the scheduler — is silently undone. The next save writes the in-memory copy back over the edit. Nothing errors; the change simply disappears.
Choice. Keep the cache. It is the right structure: one owner for the job list, no read-modify-write races between the CLI and the timer, no file locking.
The price, paid explicitly. Editing scheduler state is now an operation that requires a gateway restart to take effect, so that fact became a documented operational rule rather than a trap:

Lesson. Caching in-memory is almost always the right call; the mistake is failing to write down which caches exist. Here the cache is the reason the restart rule exists, and the rule is now a table rather than folklore.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.12 12. The backend channel: a third trigger path
text:
5.12 12. The backend channel: a third trigger path
Situation. Originally there were two ways to start a turn: a human in a chat, or a schedule. Both are person-shaped. Automated work — a long-running job, a worker, a migration — has nobody to press the button.
Choice. A channel adapter that is not a chat platform at all. It accepts signed event envelopes on a loopback endpoint and tails the jobs database for new events, and each event wakes an isolated session scoped to its job.
Why an adapter, not a hook. Because an adapter gets session isolation, the message bus, usage accounting, the agent loop, and reply handling for free. A hook would have to reimplement all of it, badly.
Why two ways in. Pushing over HTTP is simple and immediate, and a producer may not have a database. Tailing the database needs no producer changes at all: a job that already writes events gets woken for free. The tailer stores a high-watermark and starts after existing rows, so enabling it never replays history into a session.
Security posture. Refuses to start without a credential, forces a non-loopback bind address back to loopback, compares credentials in constant time, and opens the jobs database read-only.
Cost. Replies have nowhere to go. They are logged, unless the envelope names a channel to escalate to — which is the one case where a machine-initiated turn is allowed to interrupt a human.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.13 13. Jobs are a ledger, not a log file
text:
5.13 13. Jobs are a ledger, not a log file
[ops] The job tooling is workspace-side; the consumers are in the package.
Situation. Long-running delegated work needs to be observable: what is running, what is stuck, what finished, and what did it actually produce.
Rejected. Parsing the agent’s log output.
Choice. One SQLite database with a jobs table (status enum, repo, model, spec and result paths, timestamps) and a job_events table forming the timeline.
Why. A status enum is queryable; a log line is not. A structured event table supports “show me everything that happened to this job in order” with one indexed query, which is exactly what the dashboard’s detail view does. And because the events are rows, the backend tailer can select on them.
Completion detection is a file, not a pattern match. The producer writes a done-marker file when the work is genuinely finished. Nothing greps a log for a success phrase. Grepping logs is fragile in a way that is invisible until it matters: log rotation truncates the evidence, concurrent runs interleave, and a model quoting the phrase it was looking for produces a false positive. A file’s existence is a contract that cannot be misread.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.14 14. Dashboard parity means behaviour and confirmation
text:
5.14 14. Dashboard parity means behaviour and confirmation
Situation. The dashboard is supposed to be “the same assistant, in a browser”. The first attempts implemented the mechanism — an endpoint that starts a new session — and still did not match.
The chain of commits is the story:

0138361 — make the dashboard’s “new chat” archive the session the way Telegram’s /new does. Mechanism parity.
cade0bc — persist the rotation to disk, fix the mobile layout and the PWA cache headers.
9d9747c — fix the subtle one: the new-chat path was archiving a stale disk copy of the session, because the live conversation only lives in memory and is flushed opportunistically. Every message since the last save was silently dropped from the archive. The fix archives the cached session when there is one.
9d535f2 — add the success toast, so the user is told “session archived, new chat started”.

The rule. Parity is behaviour plus confirmation UX. A feature that works but does not say it happened is not done. The user must not have to open the transcript to find out whether something was saved.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.15 15. Per-session concurrency instead of one global dispatch lock
text:
5.15 15. Per-session concurrency instead of one global dispatch lock
Situation. A single lock around message dispatch meant one slow turn blocked every other conversation — including /btw side questions and background work.
Choice. Three layers, in a fixed order: a global lock for runtime hot-reload and config mutation, a semaphore capping concurrent sessions, then a per-session lock. Commit 5929cc3 and its tests cover cross-session parallelism, ordering within a session, registry cleanup when locks go idle, /stop isolation, and the global cap.
Why a lock registry rather than a single lock. Sessions are created and destroyed constantly; a fixed set of locks would leak. The registry creates a lock on first use and drops it when it is unlocked with no waiters, which is why the tests assert the registry does not grow.
Why the lock ordering is documented. Deadlock avoidance by convention is fragile. The rule — global before session, never the reverse — is written at the point of acquisition where it would be violated, and the concurrency tests are what keep the convention honest.
The same commit added guards elsewhere for the same reason: an asyncio.Lock around memory writes, the scheduler’s job list, and the subagent task registry. The lesson is that per-session concurrency does not remove the need for locking; it moves it to the objects that are actually shared.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.16 16. Restart: script for source, CLI for configuration
text:
5.16 16. Restart: script for source, CLI for configuration
Situation. After landing a change to the gateway, the running process still has the old code. Something has to restart it.
Choices. (a) Kill by pattern; (b) restart by hand; (c) a redeploy script for source and a CLI restart for configuration.
Choice. (c). The redeploy script reinstalls the package, writes a restart-request flag containing where to send the confirmation, restarts the daemon through its own CLI, and lets the new process consume the flag and send a boot notification reporting version and provider status. Configuration-only changes use the CLI restart command.
The incident that produced the rule. An ad-hoc kill by process-name pattern was run from inside a session. The pattern matched the shell command that was running the kill, so the session killed itself. Recovery took roughly eight minutes. The rule is now blunt: restart through the CLI, never by hand.
Why the flag file exists at all. Because a restart is asynchronous from the operator’s point of view. Writing “please tell me when you’re back” to disk before restarting is what turns a silent restart into an observable one — and it is why the confirmation includes the version that is now live, which is what versioning depends on.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.17 17. Versioning: the deploy log is the source of truth
text:
5.17 17. Versioning: the deploy log is the source of truth
[ops]
Situation. With an editable install and a restart-based deploy, “which code is running?” becomes a real question, not a rhetorical one.
Choice. Semantic version bumps committed alongside the change, a deploy log recording each deployed version, commit messages that reference the unit of work, and a boot notification that reports the version of the running process.
Why. The running process reports its own version at boot, and the deploy log records what was pushed when. Together they answer “is the fix live?” without anyone having to remember. Referencing the work unit in the commit message is what makes the history navigable: git log --grep finds every change belonging to a decision, and the Engineering Log at the end of this book is written from exactly that history.
Cost. Version discipline is manual. It is kept honest by bumping in the same commit as the behaviour change, never in a batch.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.18 18. Tests, and treating a green suite as a claim
text:
5.18 18. Tests, and treating a green suite as a claim
Situation. A single-operator project still accumulates enough moving parts — a scheduler, a watcher, three HTTP servers, four databases — that regressions are guaranteed without tests.
Choice. unittest-style suites under tests/, mandatory for every unit of work, plus two pieces of hygiene that matter more than usual here:

Isolation by default. An autouse fixture redirects the usage store to a per-test temporary database, so no test can write to the production ledger even if the test author forgets. The store has its own second net for the same reason.
A flaky test is a defect. A suite that must be re-run to be believed is not green, it is noisy. The rule is: re-run before trusting green; if it fails again, record it and fix it.

And the cultural half. Incidents and corrections are written down as durable facts, and the most important ones are promoted into the protected hard-lessons region of memory so trimming can never drop them. The cap-and-protect design in Chapter 3 exists because of this: the most valuable thing in the memory file is the thing that must survive.

title: 5  Decisions and Backstories
section: 5.19 What the decisions have in common
text:
5.19 What the decisions have in common
Read the list backwards and a single theme emerges: the code is the cheap part, the invariants are the expensive part.

Every cache in the system is documented as a cache, so “why did my edit vanish” is answerable.
Every trimmer protects its most valuable content, because trimming is where value silently leaks.
Every fan-out point — the bus, the API, the lock registry — has an invariant written at the point where it would be broken.
Every capability that could be asynchronous but shouldn’t, isn’t: review waits for idleness, the scheduler waits for its timer, one agent per repository waits for the last one.

The through-line from Chapter 1 is intact. The requirement was that the data flow be traceable. The decisions above are what it costs to keep that true as the system grows.

title: 6  Engineering Log
text:
6.1 How to add an entry
This is the living page of the book. Chapters 1 to 4 describe how the system works and why; this page records what changed, newest first, with the lesson attached.
It is the mechanism that keeps the book honest. A decision chapter that is never updated is a museum; this page is the changelog that forces the rest of the book to be revisited whenever something moves.
Last entry: 2026-10-04 · Entries: 5 · Newest first
Append to the top of the list, directly under this line:

title: 6  Engineering Log
text:
Pick a date (the day of the change, not the day you are writing it up).
Copy the template below verbatim and fill it in.
Make the lesson sentence the point. If the entry cannot state a rule or a correction, it is a changelog line, not a log entry.
If the change invalidates something in a chapter, fix the chapter in the same commit. A log entry that leaves the book contradicting itself is worse than no entry.
Re-render and re-run the smoke test (see doc/README.md).


6.1.1 Entry template
Copy everything between the rules below into a new ## YYYY-MM-DD — <title> section.
## YYYY-MM-DD — <short title>

**What changed.** One or two sentences. Name the subsystem and the observable
behaviour change. Reference the commit by short hash if there is one.

**Why.** The situation that made the change necessary — a limit reached, a bug
seen, a capability needed.

**Lesson / correction.** The rule that comes out of it, phrased as an instruction
to the next person (or the next run). This is the part future readers care
about.

**Where it lives.** The files that were touched, relative to the repository root.


6.1.2 House rules for entries

Evidence, not narrative. Point at code, a commit, or an observable behaviour. If neither exists, the entry is not ready.
No personal information. The same rules as the rest of the book: no names, no identifiers, no credentials, no private paths. See doc/README.md.
Corrections are welcome, mistakes are not hidden. An entry that records “this was wrong, here is the rule now” is more valuable than one that never records a mistake.
One entry per decision, not per commit. A commit that touches three files for one reason is one entry.

title: 6  Engineering Log
section: 6.2 2026-10-04 — Session topics and the backend channel (0.15.0)
text:
6.2 2026-10-04 — Session topics and the backend channel (0.15.0)
What changed. Two features in one release. First, a session topic is now carried on the reply itself: the prompt instructs the model to end every final user-facing response with exactly one trailing machine line naming a topic (or explicitly clearing it), and the gateway strips that line, applies it to session metadata, and persists it. Second, the backend channel landed — a loopback-only, token-gated event endpoint plus a read-only tailer over the jobs database, both waking isolated per-job sessions. A lightweight SQLite sessions index landed with it so listing sessions stops reading every transcript. Reference: 553c00e.
Why. Sessions had no subject line, so a long-lived conversation was unidentifiable in the dashboard and in any listing. And the assistant could only be started by a person in a chat, or on a schedule — automated work had no way to wake it.
Lesson / correction. Machine-readable lines must be stripped at the edge, before anything else touches the content, and they must never be visible in user facing text. When the model fails to emit one, the gateway treats it as a no-op rather than an error: a missing signal degrades, it does not fail. And a user-locked value must never be overwritten by a model-suggested one — that asymmetry has to be encoded, not assumed.
Where it lives. sarathy/agent/loop.py, sarathy/agent/context.py, sarathy/agent/builtin_commands.py, sarathy/channels/backend.py, sarathy/channels/manager.py, sarathy/config/schema.py, sarathy/session/manager.py.

title: 6  Engineering Log
section: 6.3 2026-09-23 — Dashboard “new chat” parity, in four commits
text:
6.3 2026-09-23 — Dashboard “new chat” parity, in four commits
What changed. The dashboard’s new-chat action was brought to parity with the chat command, in sequence: archive the session the way the chat side does (0138361), persist the rotation and fix mobile layout and cache headers (cade0bc), archive the live cached session rather than the stale on-disk copy (9d9747c), and confirm it to the user with a success toast (9d535f2).
Why. The mechanism existed and was wrong. Because the live conversation lives in memory and is only flushed to disk opportunistically, the rotation archived an old snapshot — every message since the last save was silently dropped from the archive — and never persisted the fresh session, so a reload resurrected the conversation that was supposed to be gone. Two archive files of identical size were the symptom that gave it away.
Lesson / correction. A rotation must archive what is actually in memory, not what happens to be on disk. When a component caches, the cache is the truth and the file is a lagging copy — code that reads the file to make a destructive decision is operating on stale data. And parity is behaviour plus confirmation: a feature that works but does not say it happened is not finished. Walk both products end to end; do not compare mechanisms.
Where it lives. sarathy/session/manager.py, the dashboard session view and its API handlers.

title: 6  Engineering Log
section: 6.4 2026-09-22 — Per-session concurrency replaces the global dispatch lock
text:
6.4 2026-09-22 — Per-session concurrency replaces the global dispatch lock
What changed. A single dispatch lock was replaced with three layers: a global lock for runtime hot-reload and configuration mutation, a semaphore capping concurrent sessions, and a per-session lock registry that creates locks on demand and drops them when idle. Matching guards were added around memory writes, the scheduler’s job list, and the subagent task registry. Reference: 5929cc3.
Why. One slow turn blocked every other conversation — including side questions and background work. The assistant was effectively single-lane.
Lesson / correction. Removing a global lock does not remove the need for locking; it moves the lock onto the objects that are genuinely shared. Lock ordering has to be written down at the point of acquisition, and the tests have to cover it: parallelism across sessions, ordering within a session, registry cleanup, cancellation isolation, and the global cap. A lock registry that never shrinks is a slow leak.
Where it lives. sarathy/agent/loop.py, sarathy/session/memory.py, sarathy/cron/service.py, sarathy/agent/subagent.py, tests/test_session_concurrency.py.

title: 6  Engineering Log
section: 6.5 2026-09-22 — Session epochs make “new conversation” reset the cost ledger
text:
6.5 2026-09-22 — Session epochs make “new conversation” reset the cost ledger
What changed. Usage accounting gained an epoch: every usage row records the epoch that was current at the time, a small table holds the authoritative current epoch per session, and starting a new conversation advances it. The compact usage footer now reports the cost of the current conversation rather than of all time. References: 33f455b, 3c107b1, 054a211.
Why. Cost was attributed to the session key, which lives for the whole life of a chat. Starting a new conversation did not and could not reset the number without deleting history.
Lesson / correction. Attribute to the conversation, key on the identity. Adding a dimension beat mutating history: the ledger stays append-only, and the authoritative epoch lives outside it so a crash between “advance” and “next turn” cannot desynchronise. Schema changes ship as numbered, idempotent migrations that re-check for existing columns.
Where it lives. sarathy/usage/store.py, sarathy/usage/footer.py, sarathy/agent/loop.py.

title: 6  Engineering Log
section: 6.6 2026-09-20 — Cron sessions rotate at the trim cap, and archives get retention
text:
6.6 2026-09-20 — Cron sessions rotate at the trim cap, and archives get retention
What changed. Scheduled jobs now rotate their session between runs rather than never; the check runs on both the cached and the cold-load path; cron sessions are exempt from the save-time trim so their full history reaches the archive; and prune_archives() added an explicit retention policy that keeps anything still unverified. Reference: 67a3176.
Why. A cron session reuses one stable key and was being trimmed to the cap on every save, so the length could never reach the rotation threshold. The session was reused forever on a rolling window of stale context until a run’s prompt overflowed — and the run reported success while producing nothing.
Lesson / correction. A cap and a rotation threshold are different numbers; if the cap keeps the value below the threshold, the rotation is dead code. Verify that a limit can actually be reached before relying on the behaviour behind it. Rotation points must also respect the unit of work — a cron session may rotate between runs, never mid-run, because a mid-run rotation destroys the run’s own context. And any directory that grows without a reaper needs an explicit retention policy.
Where it lives. sarathy/session/manager.py, tests/test_session_rotation.py.

title: 6  Engineering Log
text:
6.7 Seeded from the history
These five entries were written from the commit history on 2026-10-04, working backwards from the release that prompted this book. They are deliberately short and deliberately specific: the point of an entry is the lesson, and a lesson that needs three paragraphs is usually a chapter section instead. Later entries should be written at the moment the decision is made, while the reasoning is still fresh — that is the only time the “why” is fully available.
